title: Initialization and vanishing gradients
summary: Backpropagation multiplies many local factors, so gradients shrink to nothing or explode in deep networks; ten sigmoid layers cut the signal below a millionth. Starting weights must be random (to break symmetry) and scaled to the layer: variance 1/n (Xavier) or 2/n for ReLU (He) keeps signals the same size from layer to layer.
llm_link: GPT-2 scales down the initial weights of the layers that write into each block's residual path by 1/√N (N = number of residual layers), so the residual stream does not grow as dozens of blocks add to it.
key_ideas: A product of many factors below 1 vanishes; above 1 it explodes. Gradients in deep networks are such products.
Sigmoid slope ≤ ¼, so ten sigmoid layers shrink the gradient by (¼)^10 ≈ 10^-6: the vanishing gradient problem.
Summing n inputs multiplies the variance by n·Var(w), so Var(w) = 1/n keeps the signal's size steady (Xavier/Glorot 2010).
ReLU zeroes about half its inputs, so He initialisation (2015) uses Var(w) = 2/n.
Identical starting weights give identical outputs and identical gradients forever: randomness breaks the symmetry.

quiz.q: Predict the result: a gradient passes back through 10 layers that each multiply it by 0.5. Roughly what fraction survives?
quiz.explain: 0.5^10 = 1/1024, about a thousandth. Long products of factors below 1 vanish.

quiz.q: Why does a stack of sigmoid layers suffer from vanishing gradients?
options: Its slope is at most 1/4, so each layer shrinks the gradient
It makes the weights too large
quiz.explain: Each sigmoid multiplies the passing gradient by at most 1/4, so depth shrinks it geometrically.

quiz.q: A ReLU layer has 512 inputs. With He initialisation, what is the standard deviation of the weights?
quiz.explain: He initialisation sets Var(w) = 2/n, so the standard deviation is √(2/512) = √(1/256) = 1/16 = 0.0625.

quiz.q: What goes wrong if every weight in a layer starts at the same value?
options: All neurons compute the same thing, get the same gradient, and stay identical
quiz.explain: Symmetric neurons get symmetric updates, so the layer acts like a single neuron however wide it is.

quiz.q: How does GPT-2 stop its residual stream from growing as dozens of blocks add to it?
options: It scales the initial weights of the layers writing into the residual path by 1/√N
It initialises all weights to zero
quiz.explain: N is the number of residual layers; the scaling keeps the sum of many contributions from blowing up at the start of training.

problems.title: How fast does the gradient vanish?
problems.prompt:
Write chain_factor(slopes): the product of a list of local slopes, which is what backpropagation multiplies along a path. Then sigmoid_chain(zs): the product of the sigmoid's slope σ(z)(1 − σ(z)) at each pre-activation in zs.

chain_factor([0.5, 0.5, 0.5])   # 0.125
sigmoid_chain([0] * 10)          # 0.25 ** 10, about 9.5e-07

tests.name: empty path changes nothing
tests.code:
got = chain_factor([])
assert got == 1, f'a path with no layers multiplies by nothing: 1, got {got}. Start the product at 1'

tests.name: ten sigmoids at their steepest
tests.code:
got = sigmoid_chain([0] * 10)
assert abs(got - 0.25 ** 10) < 1e-15, f'each slope is 0.25 at z = 0, so the product is 0.25**10 = {0.25 ** 10:.3e}, got {got}'
assert got < 1e-6, 'that is less than a millionth'

tests.name: saturated sigmoids are worse
tests.code:
a = sigmoid_chain([0] * 5)
b = sigmoid_chain([4] * 5)
assert b < a / 1000, f'at z = 4 the slope is about 0.018, so five layers vanish far faster: got {b:.2e} vs {a:.2e}'

hints:
p = 1
for s in slopes:
    p *= s
return p
sigmoid_chain: chain_factor([sigmoid(z) * (1 - sigmoid(z)) for z in zs])

problems.title: Keep the signal alive (NumPy)
problems.prompt:
Push a batch of random inputs through 30 ReLU layers of width 256 and watch the signal's size.

  1. he_init(n_in, n_out, rng): weights of shape (n_out, n_in) from a normal distribution with standard deviation √(2 / n_in).
  2. signal_sizes(std_fn, depth, width, rng): start with X = rng.normal(size=(width, 64)) (64 examples as columns); for each layer draw W = rng.normal(size=(width, width)) * std_fn(width), set X = np.maximum(0, W @ X), and record X.std(). Return the list of stds.

The tests compare He scaling with a fixed small spread of 0.01.

tests.name: He init has the right shape and spread
tests.code:
import numpy as np
W = he_init(512, 300, np.random.default_rng(0))
assert W.shape == (300, 512), f'shape should be (n_out, n_in) = (300, 512), got {W.shape}'
assert abs(W.std() - np.sqrt(2 / 512)) < 0.003, f'std should be close to sqrt(2/512) = 0.0625, got {W.std():.4f}'

tests.name: records one size per layer
tests.code:
import numpy as np
s = signal_sizes(lambda n: np.sqrt(2 / n), 5, 64, np.random.default_rng(0))
assert len(s) == 5, f'5 layers should give 5 recorded sizes, got {len(s)}'

tests.name: He scaling keeps the signal alive
tests.code:
import numpy as np
s = signal_sizes(lambda n: np.sqrt(2 / n), 30, 256, np.random.default_rng(0))
assert 0.2 < s[-1] < 5, f'with std sqrt(2/n) the signal should stay roughly the same size after 30 layers, got {s[-1]:.3g}'

tests.name: a fixed small spread kills it
tests.code:
import numpy as np
s = signal_sizes(lambda n: 0.01, 30, 256, np.random.default_rng(0))
assert s[-1] < 1e-10, f'with std 0.01 each layer shrinks the signal, so after 30 layers it should be essentially 0; got {s[-1]:.3g}'

hints: he_init: return rng.normal(size=(n_out, n_in)) * np.sqrt(2 / n_in)

for _ in range(depth):
    W = rng.normal(size=(width, width)) * std_fn(width)
    X = np.maximum(0, W @ X)
    sizes.append(X.std())
